title: Capstone: URL shortener
summary: Connect requirements, estimates, data, caching, and failure into one defensible design.

parts.rule: Build the URL shortener in the same order as a system-design answer: scope the product, estimate traffic and storage, define APIs and data, walk write and read paths, then address the first bottleneck and failures. Every component should answer a stated requirement or a number. A complete simple design is stronger than an unexplained distributed one.
parts.why: The capstone tests whether separate concepts form one coherent system. An estimate should justify the storage choice; the access path should justify the index and cache; the consistency requirement should determine invalidation. If those decisions do not connect, the diagram is a list of technologies rather than a design.
parts.example: Scope three operations: create a short link, redirect by code, and let the owner disable it. Require p95 redirects below 100 ms and 99.9% availability; leave analytics out of the first version. Assume 10 creates and 1,000 redirects per second on average, with a 3× peak. At 10 creates per second, one year adds about 315 million rows. At roughly 500 bytes per row before indexes and replicas, that is about 160 GB of raw data. API: POST /v1/links returns code; GET /{code} returns 302; DELETE /v1/links/{code} disables it. Store links(code primary key, destination_url, owner_id, created_at, disabled_at). The create path validates the URL, generates a random 7-character base62 code, inserts with a unique constraint, and retries a collision up to 3 times. The redirect path checks cache key link:{code}; on a miss it reads the primary-key row, rejects disabled links, fills the cache, and returns 302. A 95% cache hit rate reduces 1,000 average reads per second to about 50 database reads per second. On delete, commit disabled_at, then evict the cache key; discuss the brief stale-read risk if eviction fails. Start with one relational primary plus backups and perhaps read replicas. The estimated write rate does not justify sharding yet. For failure, time out cache quickly and fall back to the database; if the database is unavailable, cached redirects may continue but creates should fail rather than acknowledge lost data.
parts.use: Use this capstone to practice a 30–45 minute answer and transitions between sections. After the baseline works, choose one deep dive—code collisions, cache invalidation, abuse prevention, or regional latency—and analyze it with the same requirements-first discipline.
parts.refuse: Do not add a queue, stream processor, sharding layer, or multi-region consensus without tying it to traffic, latency, or durability. Do not call storage “small” without doing the multiplication. Avoid a redirect design with no disabled-link or stale-cache story, and do not spend the whole interview on code generation while the main read path remains undefined.

body:
Rule. Build the URL shortener in the same order as a system-design answer: scope the product, estimate traffic and storage, define APIs and data, walk write and read paths, then address the first bottleneck and failures. Every component should answer a stated requirement or a number. A complete simple design is stronger than an unexplained distributed one.

Why it matters. The capstone tests whether separate concepts form one coherent system. An estimate should justify the storage choice; the access path should justify the index and cache; the consistency requirement should determine invalidation. If those decisions do not connect, the diagram is a list of technologies rather than a design.

Worked example. Scope three operations: create a short link, redirect by code, and let the owner disable it. Require p95 redirects below 100 ms and 99.9% availability; leave analytics out of the first version. Assume 10 creates and 1,000 redirects per second on average, with a 3× peak. At 10 creates per second, one year adds about 315 million rows. At roughly 500 bytes per row before indexes and replicas, that is about 160 GB of raw data. API: POST /v1/links returns code; GET /{code} returns 302; DELETE /v1/links/{code} disables it. Store links(code primary key, destination_url, owner_id, created_at, disabled_at). The create path validates the URL, generates a random 7-character base62 code, inserts with a unique constraint, and retries a collision up to 3 times. The redirect path checks cache key link:{code}; on a miss it reads the primary-key row, rejects disabled links, fills the cache, and returns 302. A 95% cache hit rate reduces 1,000 average reads per second to about 50 database reads per second. On delete, commit disabled_at, then evict the cache key; discuss the brief stale-read risk if eviction fails. Start with one relational primary plus backups and perhaps read replicas. The estimated write rate does not justify sharding yet. For failure, time out cache quickly and fall back to the database; if the database is unavailable, cached redirects may continue but creates should fail rather than acknowledge lost data.

[[diagram:shorten]]

When to use. Use this capstone to practice a 30–45 minute answer and transitions between sections. After the baseline works, choose one deep dive—code collisions, cache invalidation, abuse prevention, or regional latency—and analyze it with the same requirements-first discipline.

When to refuse. Do not add a queue, stream processor, sharding layer, or multi-region consensus without tying it to traffic, latency, or durability. Do not call storage “small” without doing the multiplication. Avoid a redirect design with no disabled-link or stale-cache story, and do not spend the whole interview on code generation while the main read path remains undefined.
